newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysian ringgit seen under new pressure.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysian ringgit seen under new pressure.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit is bracing for another round of selling pressure following recent speculative attacks as the market focuses on a possible overheating in the economy, analysts said on Friday.
They said the concern about the economy followed Malaysia's surprisingly high loans and monetary growth figures for June, despite steps by the central bank, Bank Negara, to curb them.
Bank Negara announced on Wednesday that broad money supply, or M3, grew by 21.9 percent year-on-year in June against 20.3 percent in May and 22.9 percent in the same month last year.
Loans growth in June rose to an annualised 30 percent from 29.5 percent at the end of May.

"The numbers helped fuse a change in views on Malaysia," said Philip Wee, regional treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore. "The focus has shifted to overheating of the economy. This will not help the ringgit which will remain under pressure."
The ringgit has been under heavy selling pressure for over a month, losing more than five percent against the U.S. dollar.
At 0845 GMT, the ringgit was at 2.6505/15 to a dollar, drawing closer to its year's low of 2.6530.
Analysts and dealers said the ringgit could weaken to 2.70 a dollar in the near term.
"I don't think the Malaysian authorities can do much about it because these are not just speculative flows. There are actual capital outflows as well," said a Singapore dealer.
Ishak Ismail, market analyst at research house I.D.E.A., said the central bank was unlikely to intervene to defend the ringgit if the fall towards 2.70 was gradual.
"If the fall is drastic, then Bank Negara will have to do something," he said.
The central bank spent $2.0-3.0 billion of its reserves in June to defend the ringgit from speculative attack.
An unexpectedly large trade deficit for June and a weak stock market have added pressure on the beleaguered ringgit.
On Monday, Malaysia reported a trade deficit of 2.8 billion ringgit ($1.1 billion) for June after a surplus of 156.2 million ringgit in May.

Capital control measures, introduced by the central bank on Sunday to cool speculation in the ringgit and push down interest rates, have rattled the stock market, driving down the benchmark index more than six percent this week.
Bank Negara ordered local banks to limit non-trade related currency swaps to $2.0 million with each overseas customer.

But analysts said the curbs, which followed stinging verbal attacks on speculators by Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, have not helped the ringgit much and are unlikely to prevent further gains in the dollar.
They said the market was already long on ringgit positions before the restriction was imposed, and offshore players accounted for the bulk of liquidity in the forward market.
Thus, a fresh attack on the ringgit could not be ruled out, they added.
"It's still possible. The focus has now moved from the region to Malaysia due to its domestic factors," said Wee of Standard Chartered Bank.
"The economy is growing at a stronger rate that what the authorities want to see, and this is worrisome," he said.
